title: A Centenary of Justice -- Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work
keywords: Appendix B: Justice Is God's Work

primary_topics: Appendix B of 'A Centenary of Justice' -- CJP's closing address 'Justice Is God's Work,' delivered March 9, 2001 to the graduates of the Philippine Judicial Academy's (Philja) Second Pre-Judicature Program at the Supreme Court Centennial Building
CJP's personal account of his 1986-1995 spiritual rebirth in the 'Bukas Loob sa Diyos' charismatic community of renewed Catholics, and how his faith shaped his entry into the judiciary

The central theological puzzle he poses -- if God is love, why does He punish, and why is a judge 'called to impose penalties'? -- resolved through the parable of a traffic-court judge who fines a young woman and then pays the fine himself, because she is his daughter (the judge as Christ; justice and love both fulfilled)

The resulting conviction that justice is both a 'human necessity' and a 'divine essentiality': because both love and justice are in God's very nature, 'to dispense quality justice is to do God's work'
sub_topics: The occasion: a Philja invitation -- 'a summons... which cannot be refused' -- from the 'respected and loved' Chancellor Ameurfina Aguinaldo Melencio Herrera, served by former colleague Justice Antonio M. Martinez, with Pre-Judicature Program chair Justice Ricardo C. Puno present

Congratulating 'the first batch to finish this Pre-Judicature Program in the first year of the first century of the new millennium'; the program is now a prerequisite to a Judicial and Bar Council recommendation for the judiciary
CJP's recollection of his own 1995 entry 'direct to the Supreme Court,' filled with 'awe and anxiety' and 'intellectual and spiritual soul-searching'

The 1986-1995 spiritual rebirth: he and his wife joined 'Bukas Loob sa Diyos,' a charismatic community of renewed Catholics, through a marriage encounter, a 'Life in the Spirit' seminar and retreats; they read and reread the Bible, became servant-leaders, and 'came to know Him and to experience His love'
His learned dependence on God for 'all my needs,' anchored in Isaiah 55:8-9 ('My thoughts are not your thoughts') and Romans 8:28 ('God makes all things work for the good of those who love Him')

The Lord's core teaching of love (love God and neighbor; love even one's enemies, Matthew 5:44-48), against which CJP poses his hard question: why does a God of love punish, allow affliction, and call a judge to impose penalties?

The traffic-court parable: a judge fines a repentant over-speeding young woman P300, then quietly removes his robe and pays the fine himself -- because the lawbreaker is his daughter -- so 'justice was served, and so was love'; the judge is Christ and the young lady is each of us

The theological resolution: because justice is in God's nature, He 'cannot refuse to impose the sanction of His own law' without violating His nature; but being love personified, He sent His Son, who 'atoned for our sins and owned the punishment meant for us,' fulfilling both justice and love

The closing charge: the rendition of justice is 'not only a human necessity; it is a divine essentiality' -- when judges give people their due fairly and speedily, 'without fear or favor,' they 'really do the work of the Lord,' so 'to dispense quality justice is to do God's work'

notable_anecdotes: The judge who paid the fine: CJP's central parable has a traffic-court judge fine a repentant young woman P300, then remove his robe, go to the cashier and pay it himself -- because the lawbreaker is his daughter -- so that 'justice was served, and so was love'; the judge, he says, is Christ and the young lady is each of us.

A Philja 'summons': CJP jokes that an invitation from Chancellor Ameurfina Melencio Herrera 'partakes of the nature of a summons,' refusable only 'on pain of... contempt,' and that justices who brave 'lynch mobs' and 'presidential tyrants' nonetheless 'sweat bullets' over the respected and beloved chancellor.

A spiritual rebirth before the bench: CJP discloses that from 1986 to 1995 he and his wife underwent a 'spiritual rebirth' in the Bukas Loob sa Diyos community -- a marriage encounter, a 'Life in the Spirit' seminar, retreats -- becoming servant-leaders, the faith journey he carried into the Court in 1995.

The hard question: confronting why a God of love permits 'calamity, cruelty, poverty and affliction' -- and why he himself was 'called to impose penalties' -- CJP frames the whole address as the working-out of that puzzle, resolved through Christ's atonement uniting justice and love.

one_paragraph_summary: Appendix B of 'A Centenary of Justice' reproduces CJP's closing address 'Justice Is God's Work,' delivered March 9, 2001 to the graduates of the Philippine Judicial Academy's Second Pre-Judicature Program. After warmly describing a Philja invitation from the 'respected and loved' Chancellor Ameurfina Melencio Herrera as 'a summons... which cannot be refused,' CJP recalls his own 1995 entry 'direct to the Supreme Court' and the 'spiritual soul-searching' it prompted. He discloses that from 1986 to 1995 he and his wife underwent a spiritual rebirth in the 'Bukas Loob sa Diyos' charismatic community -- through a marriage encounter, a 'Life in the Spirit' seminar and retreats -- becoming servant-leaders and learning to depend on God, anchored in Isaiah 55 ('My thoughts are not your thoughts') and Romans 8:28. Against the Lord's core teaching of love (love God, neighbor and even one's enemies), he poses a hard question: if God is love, why does He punish, and why is a judge called to impose penalties? He answers with a parable -- a traffic-court judge fines a repentant young woman, then removes his robe and pays the fine himself, because she is his daughter, so that 'justice was served, and so was love.' The judge, CJP says, is Christ, who, because justice is in God's nature, could not waive the sanction of His own law, yet, being love personified, sent His Son to atone for and 'own the punishment meant for us' -- fulfilling both justice and love. He closes by charging the new judges that the rendition of justice is 'not only a human necessity; it is a divine essentiality': when they give people their due 'fairly and speedily, without fear or favor,' they do the work of the Lord, for 'to dispense quality justice is to do God's work.'
